flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me about a time a child was having a really hard moment emotionally. What did you notice about what they were feeling, and how did you respond?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q3 Attempt 1]
No. When I was a teacher aide, I used to work with autistic kids and one of the little boy, he was non-verbal, so he easily got frustrated because he couldn't express his feelings. So as I was with him through the day, I could understand what he was trying to say. So I would come to him and talk what he was trying to say and he would confirm that what he wanted. But he usually got frustrated and we wanted to leave the classroom and we had to do something. So I would just like calmly look at him and say, like, do you want to go to the bathroom so we can walk a little bit? He used to love washing his hands, so this would make him calm down.

flow_transcript_slices.question: Imagine you’re caring for a child who clearly does not want to be touched during a routine task, like diapering, helping with clothing, or guiding them physically. They are pulling away or saying no. Walk me through exactly what you would do, step by step
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q5 Attempt 1]
If a child is being like that with the diaper change, I would start distracting them first to make them stop crying first, like talking peek-a-boo or where's your feet, where's your hand or give them something to distract them and after the child is calm down and happy again, I would go back to the changing routine and I would explain, I would just change your diaper really quick, I would just clean you and then we can go back to play or eat or whatever is next on the routine.
